{{Short description|Concept category theory (mathematics)}}
In [[mathematics]], in particular in [[category theory]], the '''lifting property''' is a property of a pair of [[morphism (category theory)|morphism]]s in a [[category (mathematics)|category]]. It is used in [[homotopy theory]] within [[algebraic topology]] to define properties of morphisms starting from an explicitly given class of morphisms. It appears in a prominent way in the theory of [[model categories]], an axiomatic framework for [[homotopy theory]] introduced by [[Daniel Quillen]]. It is also used in the definition of a [[factorization system]], and of a [[weak factorization system]], notions related to but less restrictive than the notion of a model category. Several elementary notions may also be expressed using the lifting property starting from a list of (counter)examples.

==Formal definition==
A morphism <math>i</math> in a category has the ''left lifting property'' with respect to a morphism <math>p</math>, and <math>p</math> also has the ''right lifting property'' with respect to <math>i</math>, sometimes denoted <math>i\perp p</math> or <math>i\downarrow p</math>, iff the following implication holds for each morphism <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> in the category:

* if the outer square of the following diagram commutes, then there exists <math>h</math> completing the diagram, i.e. for each <math>f:A\to X</math> and <math>g:B\to Y</math> such that <math>p\circ f = g \circ i</math> there exists <math>h:B\to X</math> such that <math>h\circ i = f</math> and <math>p\circ h = g</math>.

::[[File:Model_category_lifting.png|alt=A commutative diagram in the shape of a square with an anti-diagonal line, which graphically representing the relations stated in the preceding text. There are four letters representing vertices, here listed from left to right, then from top to bottom order, which are "A" (the top-left corner of the square), "X" (the top-right corner of the square), "B" (the bottom-left corner of the square), and "Y" (the bottom-right corner of the square). Additionally, there are five arrows which connect these letters, listed here using the same order as before: a solid-stroke, left to right arrow labeled "f" from A to X (the top-side line of the square); a solid-stroke, top to bottom arrow labeled "i" from A to B (the left-side line of the square); a dotted-stroke, bottom-left to top-right arrow labeled "h" from B to X (the anti-diagonal line of the square); a solid-stroke, top to bottom arrow labeled "p" from X to Y (the right-side line of the square); and a solid-stroke, left to right arrow labeled "g" from B to Y (the bottom-side line of the square).|center]]

This is sometimes also known as the morphism <math>i</math> being ''orthogonal to'' the morphism <math>p</math>; however, this can also refer to
the stronger property that whenever <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are as above, the diagonal morphism <math>h</math> exists and is also required to be unique.

For a class <math>C</math> of morphisms in a category, its ''left orthogonal'' <math>C^{\perp \ell}</math> or <math>C^\perp</math> with respect to the lifting property, respectively its ''right orthogonal'' <math>C^{\perp r}</math> or <math>{}^\perp C</math>, is the class of all morphisms which have the left, respectively right, lifting property with respect to each morphism in the class <math>C</math>. In notation,

:<math display="block">\begin{align}
C^{\perp\ell} &:= \{ i \mid \forall p\in C, i\perp p\} \\
C^{\perp r} &:= \{ p \mid \forall i\in C, i\perp p\}
\end{align}</math>

== Properties ==

Taking the orthogonal of a class <math>C</math> is a simple way to define a class of morphisms excluding [[Isomorphism#Category_theoretic_view|non-isomorphisms]] from <math>C</math>, in a way which is useful in a [[diagram chasing]] computation.

In the category '''Set''' of [[Set (mathematics)|sets]], the right orthogonal <math>\{\emptyset \to \{*\}\}^{\perp r}</math> of the simplest [[Surjective|non-surjection]] <math>\emptyset\to \{*\}</math> is the class of surjections. The left and right orthogonals of <math>\{x_1,x_2\}\to \{*\},</math> the simplest [[Injective|non-injection]], are both precisely the class of injections, 

:<math display="block">\{\{x_1,x_2\}\to \{*\}\}^{\perp\ell} = \{\{x_1,x_2\}\to \{*\}\}^{\perp r} = \{ f \mid f \text{ is an injection } \}.</math>

It is clear that <math>C^{\perp\ell r} \supset C</math> and <math>C^{\perp r\ell} \supset C</math>. The class <math>C^{\perp r}</math> is always closed under retracts (that is, if <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are objects, <math>C \perp Y</math>, and <math>X</math> is a [[Retract (category theory)|retract]] of <math>Y</math>, then <math>C \perp X</math>), [[Pullback (category theory)|pullbacks]], (small) [[Product (category theory)|products]] (whenever they exist in the category) & composition of morphisms, and contains all isomorphisms (that is, invertible morphisms) of the underlying category. Meanwhile, <math>C^{\perp \ell}</math> is closed under retracts, [[Pushout (category theory)|pushouts]], (small) [[Coproduct (category theory)|coproducts]] & transfinite composition ([[filtered colimit]]s) of morphisms (whenever they exist in the category), and also contains all isomorphisms.

Let <math>i</math>, <math>j</math>, and <math>k</math> be morphisms such that <math>i \circ j</math> exists. Then:

* If <math>i \circ j \perp k</math> and <math>j</math> is an [[Epimorphism|epimorphism]], then <math>i \perp k</math>.

* If <math>k \perp i \circ j</math> and <math>i</math> is a [[Monomorphism|monomorphism]], then <math>k \perp j</math>.

These two properties are useful when the category is equipped with a [[Factorization system|weak factorisation system]] consisting of epimorphisms and monomorphisms.

==Examples==
A number of notions can be defined by passing to the left or right orthogonal several times starting from a list of explicit examples, i.e., as <math>C^{\perp\ell}, C^{\perp r}, C^{\perp\ell r}, C^{\perp\ell\ell}</math>, etc., where <math>C</math> is a given class of morphisms. A useful intuition is to think that the left and right lifting properties against a class <math>C</math> are a way of expressing a ''negation'' of some property of the morphisms in <math>C</math>. In this vein, performing a "double negation" can be seen as a kind of "closure" or "completion" procedure.

=== Elementary examples in various categories ===

{{Citation needed|reason=A reference is needed for these examples.|date=January 2026}}

==== In '''Set''' ====

Let <math>1</math> denote any fixed [[Singleton (mathematics)|singleton set]], such as <math>\{0\}</math>, and let <math>2</math> denote any fixed set with two elements, such as <math>\{0,1\}</math>.

* If <math>i : 1 \to 2</math> denotes either of the two functions from <math>1</math> to <math>2</math>, then <math>\{i\}^{\perp l} = \{i\}^{\perp r}</math> is the class of [[Surjective function|surjections]].

* If <math>j: 2 \to 1</math> is the unique function from <math>2</math> to <math>1</math>, then <math>\{j\}^{\perp r} = \{j\}^{\perp l}</math> is the class of [[Injective function|injections]].

==== In the category of [[Module (mathematics)|modules]] over a commutative ring R ====

Let <math>0</math> denote the [[Zero module|zero module]] and for each <math>R</math>-module <math>M</math>, let <math>0 \to M</math> and <math>M \to 0</math> denote the two unique morphisms between <math>0</math> and <math>M</math>.

* <math>\{0\to R\}^{\perp r}</math> is the class of surjective module homomorphisms.

* <math>\{R\to 0\}^{\perp r}</math> is the class of injective module homomorphisms.

* A module <math>M</math> is [[Projective module|projective]] if and only if <math>0\to M</math> is in <math>\{0\to R\}^{\perp rl}</math>.

* A module <math>M</math> is [[Injective module|injective]] if and only if <math>M\to 0</math> is in <math>\{R\to 0\}^{\perp rr}</math>.

==== In the category of [[Group (mathematics)|groups]] ====

Let <math>\Z</math> denote the infinite [[Cyclic group|cyclic group]] of [[Integer|integers]] under addition.

* <math>\{0\to \Z\}^{\perp r}</math> is the class of surjective group homomorphisms.

* <math>\{\Z \to 0\}^{\perp r}</math> is the class of injective group homomorphisms.

* A group <math>F</math> is a [[free group]] if and only if <math>0\to F</math> is in <math>\{0\to \Z \}^{\perp rl}</math>.

* A group <math>A</math> is [[Torsion (algebra)|torsion-free]] if and only if <math>0\to A</math> is in <math>\{ n \Z\to \Z : n>0 \}^{\perp r}</math>.

* A [[subgroup]] <math>A</math> of a group <math>B</math> is [[Pure subgroup|pure]] if and only if <math>A \to B</math> is in <math>\{ n\Z\to \Z : n>0 \}^{\perp r}</math>.

For a [[finite group]] <math>G</math>{{Clarify|reason=Which of the following points require G to be a finite group? Do the points referring to a group H also require H to be finite?|date=January 2026}}, 

* <math>\{0\to {\Z}/p{\Z}\} \perp 1\to G</math> iff the [[Order (group theory)|order]] of <math>G</math> is prime to <math>p</math> iff <math>\{{\Z}/p{\Z} \to 0\} \perp G\to 1</math>.

* <math>G\to 1 \in (0\to {\Z}/p{\Z})^{\perp rr}</math> iff <math>G</math> is a [[p-group|<math>p</math>-group]].

* <math>H</math> is nilpotent iff the diagonal map <math>H\to H\times H</math> is in <math>(1\to *)^{\perp\ell r}</math> where <math>(1\to *)</math> denotes the class of maps <math>\{ 1\to G : G \text{ arbitrary}\}</math>.

* a finite group <math>H</math> is [[Soluble group|soluble]] iff <math>1\to H</math> is in <math display="block">\{0\to A : A\text{ abelian}\}^{\perp\ell r}=\{[G,G]\to G : G\text{ arbitrary } \}^{\perp\ell r}.</math>

==== In the category of topological spaces ====

Let <math>\{0,1\}</math> and <math>\{0\leftrightarrow 1\}</math> denote a two-element set with the [[Discrete space|discrete]] topology and the [[Trivial topology|indiscrete]] topology, respectively. Let <math>\{0\to 1\}</math> denote the [[Sierpinski space]] of two points, in which the set <math>\{0\}</math> is open (and not closed) and the set <math>\{1\}</math> is closed (and not open), and let <math>\{0\}\to \{0\to 1\}, \{1\} \to \{0\to 1\}</math>, etc. denote the obvious embeddings.

* A space <math>X</math> is a [[Kolmogorov space|T<sub>0</sub> space]] if and only if <math>X\to \{*\}</math> is in <math>(\{0\leftrightarrow 1\} \to \{*\})^{\perp r}</math>.{{Clarify|reason=What does {*} mean? Does it denote the singleton space, or is it a shorthand for quantifying the statement over all topological spaces?|date=January 2026}}

* A space <math>X</math> is a [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub> space]] if and only if <math>\emptyset\to X</math> is in <math>( \{0\to 1\}\to \{*\})^{\perp r}</math>.

* <math>(\{1\}\to \{0\to 1\})^{\perp l}</math> is the class of maps with [[Dense set|dense]] [[Image (mathematics)|image]].

* <math>(\{0\to 1\}\to \{*\})^{\perp\ell}</math> is the class of maps <math>f:X\to Y</math> such that the [[Topological_space#Definitions|topology]] on <math>A</math> is the pullback of topology on <math>B</math>, i.e. the topology on <math>A</math> is the topology with least number of open sets such that the map is [[Continuous_function#Continuous_functions_between_topological_spaces|continuous]],

* <math>(\emptyset\to \{*\})^{\perp r}</math> is the class of surjective maps, 

* <math>(\emptyset\to \{*\})^{\perp r\ell}</math> is the class of maps of form <math>A\to A\cup D</math> where <math>D</math> is discrete,

* <math>(\emptyset\to \{*\})^{\perp r\ell\ell} = (\{a\}\to \{a,b\})^{\perp\ell}</math> is the class of maps <math>A\to B</math> such that each [[Connected component (topology)|connected component]] of <math>B</math> intersects <math>\operatorname{Im} A</math>,

* <math>(\{0,1\}\to \{*\})^{\perp r}</math> is the class of injective maps,

* <math>(\{0,1\}\to \{*\})^{\perp\ell}</math> is the class of maps <math>f:X\to Y</math> such that the [[preimage]] of a [[Connected space|connected]] closed [[Open set|open subset]] of <math>Y</math> is a connected closed open [[subset]] of <math>X</math>, e.g. <math>X</math> is connected iff <math>X\to \{*\}</math> is in <math>(\{0,1\} \to \{*\})^{\perp\ell}</math>,

* for a connected space <math>X</math>, each continuous function on <math>X</math> is bounded iff <math>\emptyset\to X \perp \cup_n (-n,n) \to \R</math> where <math>\cup_n (-n,n) \to \R</math> is the map from the [[disjoint union]] of open intervals <math>(-n,n)</math> into the [[real line]] <math>\mathbb{R},</math>

* a space <math>X</math> is [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] iff for any injective map <math>\{a,b\}\hookrightarrow X</math>, it holds <math>\{a,b\}\hookrightarrow X \perp \{a\to x \leftarrow b \}\to\{*\}</math> where <math>\{a\leftarrow x\to b \}</math> denotes the three-point space with two [[isolated point|open points]] <math>a</math> and <math>b</math>, and a [[closed point]] <math>x</math>,

* a space <math>X</math> is [[normal space|perfectly normal]] iff <math>\emptyset\to X \perp [0,1] \to \{0\leftarrow x\to 1\}</math> where the open interval <math>(0,1)</math> goes to&nbsp;<math>x</math>, and <math>0</math> maps to the point <math>0</math>, and <math>1</math> maps to the point <math>1</math>, and <math>\{0\leftarrow x\to 1\}</math> denotes the three-point space with two closed points <math>0, 1</math> and one open point <math>x</math>.

==== In the category of [[metric space]]s with [[uniformly continuous]] maps ====

* A space <math>X</math> is [[Complete metric space|complete]] iff <math>\{1/n\}_{n \in \N} \to \{0\}\cup \{1/n\}_{n \in \N} \perp X\to \{0\}</math> where <math>\{1/n\}_{n \in \N} \to \{0\}\cup \{1/n\}_{n \in \N}</math> is the obvious inclusion between the two subspaces of the real line with [[induced metric]], and <math>\{0\}</math> is the metric space consisting of a single point,

* A subspace <math>i:A\to X</math> is closed iff <math>\{1/n\}_{n \in \N} \to \{0\}\cup \{1/n\}_{n \in \N} \perp A\to X.</math>

===Examples of lifting properties in algebraic topology===
A map <math>f:U\to B</math> has the ''path lifting property'' iff <math>\{0\}\to [0,1] \perp f</math> where <math>\{0\} \to [0,1]</math> is the inclusion of one end point of the closed interval into the interval <math>[0,1]</math>.

A map <math>f:U\to B</math> has the [[homotopy lifting property]] iff <math>X \to X\times [0,1] \perp f</math> where <math>X\to X\times [0,1]</math> is the map <math>x \mapsto (x,0)</math>.

===Examples of lifting properties coming from model categories===
Fibrations and cofibrations.

* Let '''Top''' be the category of [[topological space]]s, and let <math>C_0</math> be the class of maps <math>S^n\to D^{n+1}</math>, [[embedding]]s of the boundary <math>S^n=\partial D^{n+1}</math> of a ball into the ball <math>D^{n+1}</math>. Let <math>WC_0</math> be the class of maps embedding the upper semi-sphere into the disk. <math>WC_0^{\perp\ell}, WC_0^{\perp\ell r}, C_0^{\perp\ell}, C_0^{\perp\ell r}</math> are the classes of fibrations, acyclic cofibrations, acyclic fibrations, and cofibrations.<ref>{{cite book | last = Hovey | first = Mark |title = Model Categories | url = https://archive.org/details/arxiv-math9803002 }} Def. 2.4.3, Th.2.4.9</ref>

* Let '''sSet''' be the category of [[simplicial set]]s. Let <math>C_0</math> be the class of boundary inclusions <math>\partial \Delta[n] \to \Delta[n]</math>, and let <math>WC_0</math> be the class of horn inclusions <math>\Lambda^i[n] \to \Delta[n]</math>. Then the classes of fibrations, acyclic cofibrations, acyclic fibrations, and cofibrations are, respectively, <math>WC_0^{\perp\ell}, WC_0^{\perp\ell r}, C_0^{\perp\ell}, C_0^{\perp\ell r}</math>.<ref>{{cite book | last = Hovey | first = Mark |title = Model Categories | url = https://archive.org/details/arxiv-math9803002 }} Def. 3.2.1, Th.3.6.5</ref>

* Let <math>\mathbf{Ch}(R)</math> be the category of [[chain complex]]es over a [[commutative ring]] <math>R</math>. Let <math>C_0</math> be the class of maps of form
:: <math display="block">\cdots\to 0\to R \to 0 \to 0 \to \cdots \to \cdots \to R \xrightarrow{\operatorname{id}} R \to 0 \to 0 \to \cdots,</math>
: and <math>WC_0</math> be
:: <math display="block">\cdots \to 0\to 0 \to 0 \to 0 \to \cdots \to \cdots \to R \xrightarrow{\operatorname{id}} R \to 0 \to 0 \to \cdots.</math>
:Then <math>WC_0^{\perp\ell}, WC_0^{\perp\ell r}, C_0^{\perp\ell}, C_0^{\perp\ell r}</math> are the classes of fibrations, acyclic cofibrations, acyclic fibrations, and cofibrations.<ref>{{cite book | last = Hovey | first = Mark |title = Model Categories | url = https://archive.org/details/arxiv-math9803002 }} Def. 2.3.3, Th.2.3.11</ref>
